addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)

Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, use `list_tables` to understand the existing structure
- When debugging issues, start with `get_logs` and `get_advisors` before making changes
- Use `get_project_url` and `get_publishable_api_key` when helping users configure client-side integrations

If you have access to a local development environment with a filesystem and shell:
- Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance: `npx skills add supabase/agent-skills` (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/ai-skills.md)
- Use the Supabase CLI (`supabase`) for local development workflows such as starting a local stack, managing migrations, and running edge functions locally (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development.md)

- implement: Pipeline completo de implementação: resolve o input (texto, plano ou link), garante um plano APROVADO via /refine, e dispara o workflow de implementação wave-based (agente fresco por onda + ledger persistente) que commita, verifica e abre o PR — com decisões autônomas documentadas. Ao final, auto-encadeia /review-fix-loop (desligável com 'no-review').
- refine: Transforma um pedido bruto (texto, arquivo de plano ou link — GitHub issue/PR, Jira, Slack) em um plano APROVADO com Contract block, decidindo sozinha se entrevista o usuário, se ilustra outcomes críticos para confirmação e se o risco exige /deep-plan antes da implementação. Substitui o plan mode interativo; usada isoladamente ou como etapa 1 do /implement.
- review-fix-loop: Loop review→fix em contexto limpo sobre um PR aberto: revisa (espelho da GitHub Action de code review da Anthropic, ou deep-review com 8 lentes + enumeração de facetas quando a mudança é complexa/money/deep-planned), concilia com comentários e reviews já postados no PR, posta o review consolidado no GitHub, e um agente fixer endereça os pontos (commit+push, atualiza descrição, responde quando diverge). Round 1 em largura, rounds seguintes em profundidade (validador + fix-diff + re-enumeração); repete até exaustão — 0 High/Blocker em round de largura com enumeração seca (cap 5 rounds) — + uma rodada final para Medium/Low.
- deep-plan: Planning-time mirror of deep-review: fills and adversarially refutes a plan-contract (interaction matrix, dimension table, precondition diff) from design intent + the live codebase, before code exists. Auto-engages in plan mode for sensitive-domain status/lifecycle/flow-replacement changes; self-tiers to a light inline pass for trivial or non-sensitive plans.
- deep-review: Perform a thorough code review using parallel domain-specialized agents and core business tenets. Accepts a PR number/URL, branch name, commit SHA, or reviews current local changes by default.
- verify: Run after any code change. Runs the repo's configured format/lint/build/test pipeline with a fix loop until it's green, then reports honestly. Use when the user asks to verify, build, run tests, or confirm a change is sound — and proactively after editing code.
- verify-plan: Reconcile an implementation against the plan that specified it — flags dropped commitments (coverage), changed predicates/values (fidelity), and unplanned logic (scope-creep). Cheap, plan-grounded; run before opening a PR or per-commit during long implementations. Not a bug hunt — use /deep-review for emergent-interaction coverage.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review

{"body":"Part of #35 (section 3, enhancements 10 + 15 partial). No dependencies. Same philosophy as #28, extended from the Demos host to games.

## The picture

The shipped game was built by a loop: run headlessly, drive with a scripted replay, capture frames, LOOK at them, fix, repeat. Three debug-module holes were found and filled making that loop real.

## 1. Raw frame capture — because PNG capture *lies about motion*

One PNG encode costs ~50 ms against a 16.6 ms frame budget. The insidious part is not slowness: MonoGame's fixed timestep responds by running **four simulation updates per draw**, so the game plays correctly but capture tops out at ~15–26 fps and any clip made from it judders — you cannot tell a capture artefact from a gameplay bug, which defeats the point of looking.

`CaptureFormat.Raw` dumps RGBA via `MemoryMarshal.AsBytes` — a memcpy, no encode — sustaining **~59.8 fps at 1280x720**, with byte accounting, a full-disk stop, and a frame cap (3.5 MiB/frame; a 20 s take is 4.2 GB, so `_MAX_FRAMES` is not optional). `FromEnvironment` becomes the SINGLE owner of the env contract (`MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT=1|png|raw`, `_INTERVAL`, `_MAX_FRAMES`) — "a second reader of it would be a second dialect". An `AnnotateFilename` hook (PNG mode) lets callers stamp game-time/positions into filenames — "find the frame where she reaches the boss" becomes an `ls`, not a scrub.

## 2. `ColliderDebugSystem`: `Filter` + `Flash`

The overlay was all-or-nothing: over a tile world, hundreds of baked terrain colliders bury the three you care about — `Filter` is a predicate. And a one-frame contact is invisible to the eye — `Flash(entity)` blinks a collider white for a beat, caller-driven deliberately so resting contacts do not strobe. The game wired damage events to it: "did the hitbox actually touch him?" became visible.

## 3. `CursorPositionSystem.SkipDerivation`

The missing mouse half of input replay: `SkipHardwareRead` (already upstream) lets a replay inject cursor input, but the position system then *recomputes* screen→world each frame and clobbers the injection. One flag completes the story.

## Future (recorded, deliberately out of scope): encoded clip capture

Raw mode is the VERIFICATION tool — exact pixels (colour-run measurements), deterministic cost (an encoder's CPU contention perturbs the frame budget being profiled), scriptable indexing. Social-media clips are a different master, and two cheap paths exist when someone wants them:

1. **Desktop:** pipe raw frames into **the MGCB-bundled ffmpeg** (the engine already ships it; the game's audio tooling already locates it) on a background thread — 4.2 GB → ~50 MB, real time. Work: a double-buffer + writer thread.
2. **Web:** `canvas.captureStream()` + `MediaRecorder` — hardware-assisted WebM in ~10 lines of JS.

Modern titles use dedicated hardware encoders (NVENC/AMF/VideoToolbox) + RAM ring buffers of compressed frames; path 1 is the portable approximation. Kept out of this PR so verification and sharing do not get conflated into a tool that serves neither well.

## Delivery

- [ ] Port `ScreenshotCaptureSystem` raw mode + `FromEnvironment` + `AnnotateFilename` (debug)
- [ ] Port `ColliderDebugSystem` `Filter`/`Flash`/`FlashSeconds` (debug)
- [ ] Port `CursorPositionSystem.SkipDerivation` (cursor)
- [ ] Docs: the capture env contract, the disk-cost table, and the raw-vs-encoded rationale above
- [ ] Test: raw mode sustains full-rate capture under load (assert frame spacing), stops at the cap and on disk exhaustion; filter narrows the overlay; an injected cursor position survives the frame

Reference implementation: `roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj` → `Gmtk2026.Core/MonoDreams/debug/System/ScreenshotCaptureSystem.cs`, `debug/System/ColliderDebugSystem.cs`, `cursor/System/CursorPositionSystem.cs`.

**Value on its own:** the agentic build-verify loop that shipped this game becomes engine equipment — capture that does not lie, contacts you can see, replays that own the mouse.
","comments":[],"labels":[],"title":"debug/cursor: self-verification toolkit — raw 60fps capture, collider flash, replayable cursor"}

1	# MonoDreams — Core Tenets
2	
3	> The invariants and design principles that hold across the engine.
4	> Read this before working on MonoDreams — most of what looks surprising in
5	> the code is consistent with one of these tenets. AI coding agents should
6	> load this file as context for any non-trivial task in the repo.
7	
8	## 1. Framework, not library
9	
10	MonoDreams is to game devs what Spring is to web devs: the framework owns
11	the heavy lifting (rendering, camera, physics, level loading, spawning),
12	the developer owns the gameplay code, and the price of full control is
13	embracing ECS. The competitive position is between **bare MonoGame** (too
14	low-level — you write the rendering loop yourself) and **Nez or similar**
15	(too loose — you give up control to get convenience).
16	
17	**Two users, equal weight.**
18	- Solo devs and small indie teams who *like writing code* and want plug'n
19	  play primitives.
20	- AI coding agents (Claude Code and similar) operating on the codebase.
21	  Docs in this repo — CORE_TENETS, premises files, CLAUDE.md — are
22	  first-class context for that user, not human-only supplementary material.
23	
24	**Key rule.** When choosing between a more specialized API and a more
25	general one, pick the general one. The same primitive should serve more
26	than one feature; if it can't, it's probably a game-shaped abstraction
27	hiding inside the framework.
28	
29	## 2. ECS purity & composition
30	
31	The architecture is composition all the way down:
32	
33	- **Components** are pure data containers. No logic, no methods beyond
34	  trivial property getters. If you reach for a method on a component, the
35	  logic belongs in a system.
36	- **Systems** are pure functions over components. A system declares the
37	  components it operates on and acts on every entity that matches. It
38	  makes **no assumption** about which other systems ran before or will
39	  run after.
40	- **Entities** are IDs that group components. They carry no state of
41	  their own.
42	- **The pipeline assembler — the screen — owns ordering.** The screen
43	  registers systems in the order they should run for that screen's
44	  intended behavior. A system that quietly depends on another system
45	  having run is a framework-level bug; the dependency belongs in the
46	  pipeline assembly, not inside the system.
47	
48	**Atomic unit of composition.** A new feature usually lands as one or
49	more new systems, sometimes paired with one new component. Components
50	are added only when there is genuinely new data to model. Net: the engine
51	should always have more systems than components.
52	
53	**Discover before creating.** Before adding a component or system,
54	search what's already there. Prefer extending an existing component to
55	creating a new one (CLAUDE.md says the same — it is repeated here because
56	this is the most common review finding). The failure mode is a plethora
57	of micro-components, each solving one feature's narrow pain, none
58	reusable.
59	
60	**Key invariant.** Public contracts — messages, components, public
61	systems — must be backed by a test or example that exercises them.
62	Contracts without a maintained use site become indistinguishable from
63	dead code, and the framework cannot signal "this is part of the API" by
64	name alone.
65	
66	**Key rule (the #1 review lens).** When a PR adds a new component or
67	system, ask: *does this evolve well as more features land, or did we
68	just solve today's pain?* A hyper-specialized addition that doesn't
69	generalize is the framework's primary failure mode. If a generalization
70	isn't obvious, propose extending an existing primitive instead.
71	
72	### Aspirational direction
73	
74	- **Declarative system dependencies.** Today, ordering is implicit in
75	  the screen's registration order. A future API would let a system
76	  declare "I expect X to have run this frame" and let the framework
77	  enforce or warn at registration time.
78	- **Modular packs.** Today the engine is one bundle. The intended
79	  end-state is Spring-style modules (`MonoDreams.Rendering`,
80	  `MonoDreams.Physics`, `MonoDreams.Dialogue`, …) that can be adopted
81	  independently. The current `MonoDreams.YarnSpinner/` is the
82	  closest prototype.
83	- **Test or example per public contract.** New messages, components, and
84	  systems should ship with at least one usage that proves the contract
85	  works and signals that it's maintained.
86	
87	## 3. Hierarchy & Transform
88	
89	`Transform` is the engine's spatial component today. It holds position,
90	rotation, scale, origin, and an optional parent link; it caches a world
91	matrix and exposes `WorldPosition` / `WorldRotation` / `WorldScale`
92	properties that walk the parent chain.
93	
94	**Key invariant — don't mix two Transform-shaped components in one
95	project.** A developer is free to write a `MyTransform` with different
96	trade-offs; what breaks the framework is **mixing** `Transform` and
97	`MyTransform` in the same world. Systems should be agnostic enough to
98	operate on either one (see §2 — systems are functions), but the bundled
99	collision, rendering, camera, and culling systems read `Transform`
100	specifically. Using a custom transform means re-implementing those
101	consumers too.
102	
103	**Two parent links, intentionally.** `Transform.Parent` is the matrix
104	link (it determines how `WorldMatrix` cascades); `ChildOf` is a
105	structural marker (it determines lifecycle and cascading disposal). The
106	split exists to support complex hierarchical UI such as a dialogue
107	panel — a single visual whose banner, avatars, text and waiting-indicator
108	move and dispose together but may not all share matrix scaling.
109	`HierarchySystem` keeps the two in sync. **This split is on the refactor
110	backlog** (§10); read both fields when reasoning about hierarchy until it
111	is consolidated.
112	
113	**Dirty propagation.** Mutating a parent's transform marks the entire
114	descendant chain dirty; `WorldMatrix` is a cached property whose getter
115	re-walks the chain when needed. Systems that read `WorldPosition` get
116	the parent-corrected value, but only if `HierarchySystem` has run in the
117	pipeline ahead of them — that's the pipeline assembler's job to arrange.
118	
119	**`Transform.Delta` and `HasMoved`.** These reflect the change between
120	two committed positions. They are meaningful only after
121	`TransformCommitSystem` has run for the *previous* frame. Today no API
122	prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; this is on the backlog as
123	"`Transform` should expose interaction methods that guarantee `Delta`
124	consistency" (§10). For now, downstream systems that depend on `Delta`
125	(notably the collision detection's swept tests) must trust the
126	assembler put `TransformCommitSystem` at the end of every frame.
127	
128	### Aspirational direction
129	
130	Collision, rendering, culling, and camera all read `Transform`
131	directly. The intended end-state is loose coupling — those modules
132	operate against any *Transform-shaped contract*, so a developer can
133	swap in `MyTransform` without re-implementing them. The framework
134	currently doesn't enforce this; treat any `MonoDreams/System/`
135	reference to `Transform` as implementation debt rather than design.
136	
137	## 4. Rendering pipeline
138	
139	The rendering pipeline is the most delicate part of the engine. Bugs
140	here are visual rather than logical, which makes them harder to debug
141	than crashes. Two rules cover most of the surface:
142	
143	**Key invariant — `DrawComponent` is the unified render component.**
144	There is one `DrawComponent` per renderable entity. Its `Type` field is
145	one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or `Mesh`, mutually exclusive.
146	Source data lives in companion structs (`SpriteInfo`, `DynamicText`,
147	`NinePatchInfo`, mesh buffers) populated by prep systems
148	(`SpritePrepSystem`, `TextPrepSystem`, `MeshPrepSystem`).
149	**Do not create new draw/render components.** Adding a new visual type
150	extends `DrawElementType` and `MasterRenderSystem`; it does not fork
151	the pipeline.
152	
153	**Key invariant — `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole renderer.** No game
154	code should call `SpriteBatch` outside the prep-then-master path. A
155	parallel render system is a framework violation — flagged by review.
156	
157	**Key rule — rendering systems run last.** In any pipeline assembly,
158	the prep-cull-sort-render module goes at the end. The recommended order
159	inside the module, from the reference assembly
160	(`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331`), is:
161	`CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` → `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem`
162	→ `MeshPrepSystem` → `MasterRenderSystem`.
163	
164	**Render targets.** Three are defined by `RenderTargetID`:
165	- **Main** — world-space, camera transform applied, **respects culling**.
166	- **UI** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
167	- **HUD** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
168	
169	The `Visible` tag is added and removed by `CullingSystem` based on the
170	camera's `VirtualScreenBounds`. Only the Main target consults it. UI and
171	HUD entities don't need `Visible`; if you put a `Visible`-gated entity
172	on UI by mistake, it will always render (which is usually the desired
173	outcome anyway — but the failure mode is the reverse: a Main-target
174	entity that never gets `Visible` because no `CullingSystem` is in the
175	pipeline, and the dev stares at an invisible sprite). The renderable
176	entity stack is therefore `EntityInfo + Transform + SpriteInfo +
177	DrawComponent + Visible` for Main, minus `Visible` for UI/HUD.
178	**This split is a known wart** (§10): `Visible` may become a property of
179	`DrawComponent` to remove the easy-to-miss tag.
180	
181	**Layer depth ownership.** Three systems write `LayerDepth` — four when a
182	screen composes scene layers — in this order: `SpritePrepSystem`
183	initializes it from the sprite's layer, the optional `SceneLayerSystem`
184	remaps each scene-layer member's depth from (layer order, within-layer
185	key) while entities on no layer pass through untouched (see §6),
186	`YSortSystem` may override it for entities on Y-sorted layers, and
187	`MasterRenderSystem` sorts on the final value. `YSortSystem` uses a
188	minimal epsilon to bias parent-child groups so children stay attached
189	to their parent's depth band. Same-layer entities with the same world Y
190	fall through to insertion order — no other tiebreaker exists; if
191	flicker becomes a problem, that's where to look.
192	
193	**Camera.** A `Camera` instance owns its virtual resolution
194	(immutable after construction) and exposes mutable zoom, position, and
195	rotation. Multiple cameras at once are explicitly supported — local
196	multiplayer or CCTV-style views. `CameraFollowSystem` is *optional*:
197	fixed-camera games or custom camera systems are valid; just don't
198	register `CameraFollowSystem` and `CullingSystem` will still read
199	whatever the `Camera` reports.
200	
201	## 5. Physics & collision
202	
203	The framework provides Newtonian-style movement, gravity, layer-based
204	collision filtering, and AABB plus convex-polygon (SAT) collision
205	detection. These pieces are independent components and systems — a
206	game can use velocity without collision, or collision without
207	gravity — and the pipeline assembler picks which to register.
208	
209	**Components.** `Velocity` carries current and last velocity vectors
210	(the delta is exposed); `RigidBody` carries mass, gravity participation,
211	kinematic flag, and freeze-axis flags. A collider is its OWN entity now
212	(colliders-as-entities): `BoxCollider` carries a centered `Size`
213	(no offset — pose comes from the collider entity's `Transform`) and
214	active layers; `ConvexCollider` carries collider-entity-local vertices,
215	world-space vertices, a broadphase AABB and active layers. `ColliderTag`
216	is auto-applied to any collider entity so detection queries can match a
217	unified tag. A collider's **body** (the entity a contact acts on) is
218	resolved via `ColliderBody.Resolve` — nearest `RigidBody`/`Velocity`
219	ancestor, else itself — and `CollisionMessage` carries both the collider
220	entities and their bodies; resolution writes corrections to the body.
221	
222	**The reference physics pipeline order**, from
223	`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–286`:
224	**Movement → Velocity → Detection → Resolution → Commit.**
225	Each stage owns one job:
226	- *Movement* — game systems write `Velocity` based on input and AI.
227	- *Velocity (`VelocitySystem`)* — apply `Velocity` to `Transform.Position`.
228	- *Detection (`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`)* — broadphase via AABB
229	  + narrowphase via SAT for `ConvexCollider`; emit `CollisionMessage`s.
230	- *Resolution (`TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` or
231	  `TransformPhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`)* — correct positions and
232	  velocities for contacts; honor `RigidBody` freeze flags.
233	- *Commit (`TransformCommitSystem`)* — finalize `LastPosition`, so the
234	  next frame's `Delta` is meaningful.
235	
236	Swept collision (the dynamic AABB-vs-AABB and convex-vs-convex tests)
237	reads `Transform.Delta`. Delta is correct only if the previous frame
238	ended with `TransformCommitSystem`. Skip `Commit` and collisions go
239	through walls — see §3.
240	
241	**`ConvexCollider.BroadPhaseAABB`.** This AABB must be refreshed when
242	the world vertices change (transform moved or rotated). Detection
243	filters on it; a stale AABB makes a real collision invisible to the
244	broadphase. The detection system updates it; if you write a system
245	that mutates a convex collider's vertices directly, refresh the
246	broadphase AABB before the next detection pass.
247	
248	**Single-threaded detection.** `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`
249	holds instance-level polygon buffers. It is intentionally not
250	thread-safe; do not register two instances or invoke it from parallel
251	contexts.
252	
253	**Multiple colliders per body (colliders-as-entities).** A collider is its
254	own entity, so a body owns N collider children — the former
255	one-collider-of-each-type-per-entity assumption is retired. Detection
256	iterates collider entities; resolution corrects each contact's body,
257	accumulating sequentially with per-message re-validation so a body hit
258	through two of its colliders in one frame is not double-corrected. Two
259	shape components on ONE entity is still not a thing (it would be a single
260	collider entity with an ambiguous shape) — give each shape its own child
261	collider entity.
262	
263	### Aspirational direction
264	
265	Collision is currently coupled to `Transform` (see §3). The intended
266	end-state is collision against any Transform-shaped contract.
267	
268	## 6. Level loading & entity spawning
269	
270	**The shipped game boots native `.mdscene` levels only** (see "Native-only
271	load" below). The LDtk (`.ldtk`) parser is now **import-only**: it runs
272	once, off the game boot, to migrate a legacy level into a native scene the
273	game then owns. The pipeline below describes that **import** path — a
274	request loads a file, the parser walks the data, and it emits
275	`EntitySpawnRequest` messages that a factory turns into entities. It is
276	composed only in the reference screen's `importMode`, never at live boot.
277	
278	**The pipeline.**
279	1. Game code publishes `LoadLevelRequest`.
280	2. `LevelLoadRequestSystem` subscribes to the message. On the import path
281	   (`enableLegacyLdtkFallback: true`) it loads the LDtk file and **adds
282	   `CurrentLevelComponent` to the world**.
283	3. The LDtk parsers (`LDtkEntityParserSystem`, `LDtkTileParserSystem`)
284	   **subscribe to `CurrentLevelComponent` being added** and parse on add.
285	4. Parsers emit `EntitySpawnRequest`s.
286	5. `EntitySpawnSystem` consumes each spawn request and dispatches to an
287	   `IEntityFactory` registered for the request's string identifier.
288	
289	**Key invariant — the LDtk parsers react to component lifecycle, not
290	to push messages.** Their pattern (subscribe to `CurrentLevelComponent`
291	added) is the engine-wide default. A test or tool that adds
292	`CurrentLevelComponent` manually triggers them just as well as the
293	regular `LoadLevelRequest` path. For new parsers, follow this pattern —
294	resist the urge to make a system "only respond when the right message
295	arrived"; that couples the system to an upstream sequence that should be
296	the assembler's choice.
297	
298	**Factory registration.** `EntitySpawnSystem` keeps a dictionary of
299	`string → IEntityFactory`. Game code registers factories at screen
300	setup time. Currently, an unregistered identifier produces a logged
301	warning and the spawn is silently dropped. **Intended behavior is to
302	throw** — this is on the backlog (§10). For now, treat the warning as a
303	high-severity signal during development.
304	
305	**Native-only load — the content-driven unification (PS5, asymmetry
306	resolved).** `LevelLoadRequestSystem` is now a **native-only** dispatcher:
307	each `LoadLevelRequest` probes for a bundled native scene
308	`Content/Levels/<id>.mdscene` via `TitleContainer` (the console-portable
309	read) and, on a hit, loads it through the generalized `SceneReaderSystem`
310	(the same native reader the editor's `LoadSceneRequest` uses —
311	reconstructing entities from serialized components, not factories). An id
312	with **no** native scene **fails loud** — there is no silent LDtk attempt.
313	Native `.mdscene` is the game's real level format: versioned in
314	`Content/Levels/`, MGCB-`/copy:`-bundled, read read-only via `TitleContainer`
315	on every platform (only the desktop editor writes, PS3). **The LDtk parser
316	is now IMPORT-ONLY machinery:** it runs once — via the import op (a headless
317	`--export-scene <id>` / `MONODREAMS_EXPORT_SCENE` dev op, or a future editor
318	toolbar action) — to re-parse a legacy level and serialize the resulting
319	world to a native `.mdscene` the game then owns; it is **not wired to live
320	game boot** (composed only in the reference screen's `importMode`). This
321	closes the parser-asymmetry backlog (§10): one content-driven load path.
322	(The Blender importer that once shared this path was retired in wave BR —
323	see §10.) Migration status: the committed
324	`Content/Levels/Blender_Level.mdscene` (a native scene originally migrated
325	from Blender) boots native; the LDtk `Level_0` is not yet migrated (its
326	~21k per-tile entities need a native tile-layer batching primitive — a
327	follow-up, §10).
328	
329	## 7. The reference pipeline
330	
331	`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331` is the gold-standard pipeline
332	assembly. Read it before composing a new screen. The recommended
333	overall order, end-to-end:
334	
335	1. **Input** — keyboard/mouse polling, `InputReplaySystem` if running
336	   under replay.
337	2. **Game logic** — game-specific systems that read input and entity
338	   state to update gameplay components (movement intent, AI decisions,
339	   dialogue state).
340	3. **Physics module** — `MovementSystem` → `VelocitySystem` →
341	   `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` →
342	   `TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` (or `…PhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`) →
343	   `TransformCommitSystem`.
344	4. **Hierarchy** — `HierarchySystem` (then `TransformCommitSystem` if
345	   children moved independently), `SizeSystem`, `LayoutSystem`.
346	5. **Camera** — `CameraFollowSystem` (optional).
347	6. **Cursor** — `CursorInputSystem`, `CursorPositionSystem`.
348	7. **Render module** — `CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` →
349	   `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem` → `MeshPrepSystem` →
350	   `MasterRenderSystem` → debug overlays.
351	
352	Each game's screen owns its own pipeline. The reference assembly is a
353	recommendation — fixed-camera games omit `CameraFollowSystem`,
354	non-physics screens skip the physics module, UI-only screens may have
355	no game logic at all. What does not change is the *shape* of the order:
356	input first, render last, with physics ahead of hierarchy and hierarchy
357	ahead of culling.
358	
359	### Aspirational direction
360	
361	A declarative system-dependencies API would let
362	`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` say "I need `VelocitySystem` before
363	me this frame" and let the framework validate the assembly. Until that
364	exists, ordering bugs are caught by review (see the `/deep-review`
365	skill at §`.claude/skills/deep-review/SKILL.md`) and by behaviour
366	tests.
367	
368	## 8. Debug & testing
369	
370	The engine provides a small set of debug primitives. They are
371	*available*, not *required* — most screens register none of them.
372	
373	**`Logger`.** A static, lock-protected singleton in
374	`MonoDreams.State.Logger`. `Initialize(outputDirectory)` must be called
375	once before use; `Shutdown()` must be called to flush. Output goes to
376	`<dir>/monodreams_<timestamp>.log` with format `[wallclock] [GT gametime]
377	[LEVEL] message`. Replaces `Console.WriteLine`. The `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`
378	environment variable redirects all debug output (logs, replay input,
379	screenshots) for test isolation.
380	
381	**Input replay.** Drop `debug/input_replay.json` in the build output
382	directory. Format: `{ startLevel, description, commands: [{ action, type,
383	time }] }`. Actions match `AInputState` names. The `startLevel` field
384	skips menus and jumps straight into the named game screen. The game
385	auto-exits when the replay finishes.
386	
387	**Screenshots.** `ScreenshotCaptureSystem` saves PNGs every 2 seconds to
388	the debug directory. Off by default; enable by setting `"screenshots":
389	true` in `input_replay.json`.
390	
391	**Headless mode — two hosts, two contracts.** There are two headless
392	paths and they do *not* do the same thing:
393	
394	- **Examples** (`dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Examples -- --headless`)
395	  creates a 1×1 off-screen window and **early-returns from `Draw`** — it
396	  runs Update-side logic at max speed but renders **nothing**. It is
397	  convenient for fast logic/replay integration tests via `GameTestRunner`
398	  but cannot observe any visual or render-path behaviour. Treat it as the
399	  logic-only path; don't rely on it for rendering correctness.
400	- **Demos** (`dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Demos -- --headless --screen
401	  <name> --frames <N> --exit`) is the **observe-and-self-verify** path
402	  (issue #28). It keeps a real `GraphicsDevice` on a hidden, full-virtual-
403	  resolution backbuffer, **renders every frame** (`Draw` is not a no-op),
404	  dumps non-blank PNGs to `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`, logs periodic live-heap
405	  samples, and self-terminates after `<N>` frames. This is the supported
406	  way for an agent to verify its own work on the demo host without a human.
407	  See the `debug` module premises ("Headless Demos renders every frame";
408	  "Headless heap samples measure the live set") and
409	  `MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`.
410	
411	A literal zero-window mode / null `GraphicsDevice` is **not** possible on
412	MonoGame DesktopGL 3.8.4 (the window hosts the GL context); a hidden
413	window that never presents is the achievable form of "headless render".
414	
415	**Testing.** `MonoDreams.Tests/` uses xUnit + the custom
416	`GameTestRunner`, which spawns the game in headless mode with a temp
417	debug directory, writes an `InputReplayPlan`, waits for exit, and
418	exposes log-assertion helpers (`AssertLogContains`,
419	`AssertLogContainsInOrder`, `GetLogLines`). The gold-standard tests
420	today are `SATCollisionTests` (pure-logic), `BlenderLevelTests`
421	(native scene boot), and `InfiniteRunnerTests` (integration).
422	
423	**No architectural tests today.** ArchUnit-style assertions
424	("`MonoDreams/Component/*.cs` must contain only data") do not exist
425	yet. Most premises in `docs/{domain}/premises.md` start their `Tests:`
426	field as `none yet`; introducing architectural tests is on the backlog.
427	
428	## 9. The editor is part of the game
429	
430	The level editor is **not a separate application** and **not a separate
431	renderer** — it is the running game under an editor run configuration.
432	There is one world, one `Camera`, and one draw stack
433	(`CullingSystem → SpritePrepSystem → YSortSystem → MeshPrepSystem →
434	TextPrepSystem → MasterRenderSystem`); the editor previews exactly what
435	the player sees because it runs that same pipeline. What changes between
436	playing and editing is not *which* pipeline runs but *which systems in
437	it are allowed to run* — a **run-state contract** the engine codifies in
438	`foundation` — and the run state is driven by a **transport**, not a
439	mode-toggle key.
440	
441	**The transport model.** Under the editor run flag (`--editor` /
442	`MONODREAMS_EDITOR=1` — the ONLY way into the editor) the shell, chrome,
443	and editor systems are **always composed and visible**; no key toggles
444	the editor away. The designer drives the game like a media player through
445	the toolbar's left-most transport buttons (or the headless
446	`Play`/`Pause`/`Restart` editor ops), owned by `EditorTransport`:
447	**Paused** = `RunMode.Edit` (game logic Freeze-gated, editing tools
448	live — the boot state under the flag), **Playing** = `RunMode.Play`
449	(the game runs inside the inset viewport; the shell stays up and the
450	transport buttons + systems panel stay interactive, but the editing
451	tools are inert — a click in the viewport belongs to the game), and
452	**Restart** = return the world to the state of the original load:
453	clear the undo history, remove the world-level level components
454	(`CurrentLevelComponent` — the LDtk parsers react to its *added* event),
455	dispose every scene entity (editor infrastructure — entities tagged
456	`EditorInfrastructureComponent` — the cursor pipeline, and
457	screen-`KeepAlive`-named infrastructure survive), re-run the screen's
458	recorded `Reload`, and land Paused. **Unsaved live edits are discarded
459	by Restart** — the standard play-mode trade-off; Save first to keep
460	them.
461	
462	**The run-state contract.** `GameState.RunMode` is one of `Play`
463	(default) or `Edit`. A system opts into run-state awareness by being
464	wrapped in a `GatedSystem` carrying an `EditTimeBehavior` policy
465	(`RunNormally` / `Freeze` / `RunPartial` / `RuntimeEditable`). Each
466	frame the gate reads `RunMode` and decides whether to forward to its
467	child: `RunNormally` runs in both modes; `Freeze` runs in `Play` only;
468	`RunPartial` and `RuntimeEditable` are reserved (today they run in both,
469	finer semantics deferred). Editor tooling is **ECS systems over this
470	gated game pipeline** — selection, gizmo, undo-apply, scene save/load,
471	and the toolbar are ordinary systems registered alongside the game's,
472	made inert while Playing by an Edit guard (the transport chrome —
473	toolbar transport buttons + systems panel — deliberately stays live in
474	both states). There is no parallel editor data model: a scene
475	round-trips by serializing the entities' components, not by re-running
476	factories.
477	
478	**Key invariant — default `Play` + opt-in gating leaves every existing
479	screen byte-identical.** `RunMode` defaults to `Play`, and only a system
480	explicitly wrapped in a `GatedSystem` changes behavior with the mode. A
481	screen that never wraps a system and never sets `Edit` behaves exactly
482	as it did before the model existed. This is what makes the run-state
483	model safe to add across all modules at once.
484	
485	**Key rule — the gating policy per system group is fixed by what editing
486	needs to see and not disturb.** Render, input, cursor, and
487	`HierarchySystem` stay live in `Edit` (`RunNormally`) — the preview must
488	keep drawing, the designer must keep clicking, and an editor's transform
489	edit must still propagate to world space the same frame. Game logic,
490	physics, collision, AI/dialogue, and `CameraFollowSystem` `Freeze` in
491	`Edit` — they would otherwise move entities out from under the designer
492	or fight the editor for the camera; in `Edit` the editor drives
493	`Camera.Position`/`Zoom` directly. Get a policy wrong and the failure is
494	silent: a frozen render module is a black screen the instant you enter
495	`Edit`; a live physics module rains gravity on entities you are trying
496	to place; a frozen `HierarchySystem` shows edits at last frame's world
497	position. The authoritative system-by-mode table is the interaction
498	matrix in the level-editor plan-contract and
499	[`docs/flows/level-editor.md`](flows/level-editor.md); the run-state
500	premises live in
501	[`MonoDreams/foundation/docs/premises.md`](../MonoDreams/foundation/docs/premises.md).
502	
503	**Editor-overlay entities are standalone.** Gizmo handles, the selection
504	highlight, and the toolbar are never `ChildOfComponent`-parented to game
505	entities, because `HierarchySystem.DisposeOrphans` runs in `Edit` and
506	would cascade-dispose them when their host entity is deleted. Deletion is
507	modeled as an undo command that snapshots the disposed sub-graph, not a
508	bare `entity.Dispose()`.
509	
510	**The editor shell is a compositing concern, not a pipeline fork.** With
511	the editor composed, the game composite renders into a smaller centered
512	viewport (`ViewportManager.SetViewportInset` — deliberately the same
513	object that inverts the mouse mapping, so picking follows for free) and
514	the editor chrome renders around it at native window resolution
515	(`RenderTargetID.Editor` + `RenderLayer.Native`). The shell is
516	**constant across transport states** — it never collapses while Playing.
517	The game pipeline itself is untouched — same passes, same targets — and
518	without the run flag nothing editor-related is constructed: zero inset,
519	no chrome layer, byte-identical to a screen without the editor. Details:
520	the `rendering` and `level-editor` premises.
521	
522	**The editor is host- and screen-agnostic, and the pipeline is
523	inspectable.** The editor does not care which host or screen is running —
524	under the editor run flag every screen of every host (a menu or a module
525	demo as much as a level) builds its pipelines through the
526	`EditorPipelineRegistrar` and composes the `EditorOverlay` over its own
527	world, declaring its own per-system edit policies at the registration
528	site (e.g. a menu freezes its button interaction in `Edit` so clicks
529	belong to the editor; a runner freezes its whole simulation block). Where
530	a screen lacks a prerequisite, the overlay supplies it (its own cursor
531	pipeline for a cursor-less screen; the `DefaultEditorKeys` key surface
532	for a host with no action mapping) or degrades gracefully (no Y-sorted
533	layer ⇒ selection picks on the final source-derived depth). The recipe
534	for wiring a new host/screen is the level-editor overview's "Adding the
535	editor to a screen/host" section. The registrar
536	is also the live inspection surface — and it owns the hierarchy: composite
537	blocks are registrar groups (`AddGroup`) with named children, built and
538	gate-wrapped by the registrar itself (DefaultEcs composites hide their
539	children, so a screen must never pre-build an opaque composite for
540	anything it wants inspectable). The editor's systems panel renders that
541	tree — every entry of both pipelines, groups indented above their
542	children, name, policy, enabled state (tri-state on groups: all/none/
543	mixed) — and toggles any of them at runtime through `SetEnabled` (leaf =
544	both-modes master switch; group = cascade over its descendant leaves), so
545	the per-system edit-mode declaration is visible and adjustable while the
546	game runs.
547	
548	**Editing produces versioned, portable, diffable levels — the persistence
549	story.** A level the editor authors is saved as a native `.mdscene` **into
550	the game's SOURCE content tree** (`Content/Levels/<id>.mdscene`), versioned
551	in git — not into the ephemeral build output. Writing is a **desktop-dev-only**
552	capability (guarded by the editor run flag + an OS check + a resolved project
553	root, resolved via `MONODREAMS_PROJECT_ROOT` or a walk-up to the `game.mdproj`
554	manifest; unresolved disables Save loudly, never crashes); **reading is
555	console-portable** — the shipped game boots a level read-only through
556	`TitleContainer` over MGCB-`/copy:`-bundled files on every platform (desktop,
557	web, consoles), native-first via `LoadLevelRequest` (§6), so straying from
558	MGCB never costs console support. The serializer is **canonical and
559	byte-stable** (deterministic bytes, stable per-entity ids ordering
560	`entities[]`), so `load → edit → save` is a fixed point and a git diff of a
561	level is meaningful. A **`game.mdproj` manifest** makes "a MonoDreams project"
562	a versionable unit (entry scene, levels dir, asset roots). A new level bundles
563	**zero-touch** — the editor appends the MGCB `/copy:` entry on first save
564	(MGCB has no glob; a build-time regen would sweep gitignored placeholder art),
565	so it boots after a normal build with no manual `.mgcb` editing. And a scene is
566	**ship-ready** (fully portable) exactly when it has **zero `file:` AssetKeys** —
567	a checkable lint (all drop-folder art graduated to MGCB content keys); the
568	committed reference levels are asserted ship-clean. The invariants live in the
569	`level-editor` and `level-loading` premises.
570	
571	**One data model — anything authored is component state on an entity,
572	singletons included; special file blocks are debt.** A scene is a set of
573	entities carrying components, and *everything the designer authors lives that
574	way* — including the singletons it is tempting to model as a special
575	top-level file block (the scene camera, and later the layer map). A `camera`
576	block, a materialized editor rig for it, bespoke edit commands, and per-mode
577	re-sync seams are **four parallel representations of one value**, and every
578	one is a place the value can silently disagree with the others. The camera is
579	the case study: three camera defects in three days (zoom edits not reaching
580	the rig or the file) all lived in that camera-only plumbing; the day the
581	camera became an ordinary `core.Camera` entity — `EntityInfoComponent("Camera")`
582	+ `TransformComponent` (one rotation, on the Transform) + `CameraComponent`
583	zoom, serialized in `entities[]` like everything else — the block, the rig,
584	the commands, and the re-sync seams all deleted, exactly as colliders stopped
585	breaking the day they became child entities (§5).
586	
587	**Corollary — Inspector-visible ⇒ Save-persisted ⇒ round-trip-owned.** If a
588	value shows up in the Inspector, Save must persist it; if Save persists it,
589	`load → save` must own it as a byte fixed point. A value that is editable but
590	not serialized (or serialized but not round-trip-stable) is a bug waiting to
591	surface as "my edit vanished on reload". The one data model is what makes this
592	hold for free: an authored value is a component, and components already
593	round-trip.
594	
595	**The extension recipe (how to add a new authored thing).** Do NOT add a file
596	block or a bespoke editor subsystem. Instead:
597	
598	1. **Define a component** with clearly named authored vs derived fields (author
599	   the source; recompute the derived — e.g. `CameraComponent.Zoom` is authored,
600	   the view matrix is derived; a collider's `Size` is authored, its world AABB
601	   derived).
602	2. **Register its serializer** (`ComponentSerializerRegistry` — engine types in
603	   `EngineComponentSerializers`, game types in the game's own registration),
604	   so it round-trips through the canonical serializer.
605	3. **Optionally add an Inspector default-initializer** so "Add ⟨component⟩"
606	   births a sane instance.
607	
608	Those three steps buy the whole authoring stack — file authoring, Inspector
609	editing, undo, dirty-tracking, prefab overrides, byte-stable diffs, and
610	Game-mode sandbox protection — **by composition, not configuration**. There is
611	no fourth step and no special case. When a value seems to *need* a file block,
612	that is the signal it wants to be a component on an entity instead. (A legacy
613	block that predates this tenet is migrated forward by the CLI umbrella
614	`monodreams migrate` — the camera block's v2→v3 lift is the reference; see the
615	`level-editor` migrator premises.)
616	
617	### Aspirational direction
618	
619	The reserved `RunPartial` / `RuntimeEditable` policies are placeholders
620	for finer edit-time behavior (a system that does reduced work, or stays
621	interactive, while editing) — they run-as-`RunNormally` today and gain
622	distinct semantics when a later wave needs them. The interaction matrix
623	is enforced by review and by the editor screen's own tests until a
624	declarative system-dependency API (§2, §7) can validate it at
625	registration time.
626	
627	## 10. Refactor backlog (named cruft)
628	
629	Carried forward from the bootstrap interview so they are not forgotten.
630	Each is either implementation debt or an aspirational direction that
631	will eventually move from "documented in CORE_TENETS" to "enforced in
632	code".
633	
634	- **`ChildOf` vs `Transform.Parent` split** (§3). Two parent links
635	  exist today; consolidation desired. Until then, read both when
636	  reasoning about hierarchy.
637	- **`Visible` as a tag** (§4). Could become `DrawComponent.Visible`.
638	  Open question: would moving it complicate the bulk add/remove
639	  pattern `CullingSystem` uses today?
640	- **`Blender_` identifier prefix / parser-asymmetry** (§6). **RESOLVED
641	  (PS5); Blender importer DELETED (wave BR).** The game boot is a single
642	  native-only dispatcher (`LevelLoadRequestSystem`): `LoadLevelRequest` →
643	  native `.mdscene` via `SceneReaderSystem`, or fail loud. The LDtk parser
644	  is import-only machinery (composed only in the reference screen's
645	  `importMode`, run by the export op), so nothing legacy runs at boot. The
646	  Blender importer that once shared the `Blender_` name-prefix dispatch was
647	  retired wholesale in wave BR (parser + data types + exporter plugin + CLI
648	  registry entry + module-count docs), so the name-prefix hack is gone
649	  end-to-end — no parser asymmetry remains. Residual: the LDtk `Level_0` is
650	  not yet migrated to native (it needs a **native tile-layer batching
651	  primitive** — a compact representation for ~21k per-tile entities, so its
652	  `.mdscene` isn't a multi-MB per-entity dump); until then it is import-only
653	  and not offered by the reference menu. When the LDtk parser too is
654	  eventually deleted, the import op moves to a standalone tool.
655	- **`EntitySpawnSystem` silent-drops unregistered factories** (§6).
656	  Intended behaviour is to throw.
657	- **`Transform.Delta` consistency not enforced** (§3). No API today
658	  prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; `Transform` should expose
659	  interaction methods that guarantee consistency.
660	- **Module-level coupling to `Transform`** (§3, §5). Collision,
661	  rendering, camera, culling all read `Transform` directly. The
662	  eventual end-state is loose coupling to any Transform-shaped
663	  contract.
664	- **Folder layout** (`Component/<subdomain>/` vs `Component/<file>/`
665	  inconsistency). Intended end-state is **modular packs** (Spring Data
666	  / Spring Security analog) — `MonoDreams.Rendering`,
667	  `MonoDreams.Physics`, etc. — that can be adopted independently.
668	- **Examples headless mode is logic-only** (§8). Its `Draw` early-returns,
669	  so it renders nothing — fine for replay/logic tests, useless for visual
670	  observation. The Demos headless path (issue #28) is the load-bearing
671	  observe-and-self-verify route and *does* render; the remaining debt is
672	  that the Examples mode is still named "headless" despite not rendering,
673	  and the two paths could eventually share one host abstraction.
674	- **No architectural tests** (§8). Most premises lack programmatic
675	  protection; review and discipline are the only enforcement today.
676	- **Declarative system dependencies** (§2, §7). A future API would let
677	  a system declare "I expect X to have run this frame" at registration
678	  time, replacing implicit-order discipline with explicit assertions.
679	- **Test or example per public contract** (§2). Several messages
680	  (`PositionChangeMessage`, `SizeChangeMessage`, `RigidBodyTouchMessage`)
681	  are exposed but may be leftovers without active consumers. Every
682	  contract should ship with at least one usage.
